subject: health
unitTitle: Substance Use, Community Risk, and Harm-Reduction Literacy
title: Launch and diagnostic: individual risk versus population-level risk
essentialQuestion: What does the evidence say actually reduces harm, and what only sounds tough?
keyPoints: Individual risk describes a person’s probability under specific conditions, while population risk describes patterns across groups; one cannot be substituted for the other without context.
A durable plan names the goal, constraints, feasible options, support and backup routes, plus the evidence or condition that should trigger review and revision.

For individual risk versus population-level risk, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support.
privacySafeScenario: Evaluate two fictional community prevention campaigns against stated evidence criteria, then redesign the weaker one and state how its effect would be measured.
studentTask: Build a decision organizer for a fictional person working on individual risk versus population-level risk. Record the goal, two influences or constraints, two options, the safest feasible choice, a support or backup route, and the evidence that would trigger a later revision.
knowledgeCheck: In two or three sentences, explain the most important distinction in individual risk versus population-level risk; use one lesson fact and name the evidence, safety check, or support route that makes the explanation dependable.
completionCriteria: The response completes every named part of the individual risk versus population-level risk task using the supplied fictional or public case.
The response uses at least two accurate details from the lesson instruction and distinguishes evidence from assumption.
The response gives a safe, feasible next step or support route and does not depend on private disclosure, body comparison, or recorded media proof.
adaptationChoices: Evaluation and redesign may be written, storyboarded, dictated, or completed on a supplied criteria template.
extensionChallenge: Apply individual risk versus population-level risk under a new constraint, compare two approaches, or explain the idea to someone else with an original fictional example, without completing another learner's graded work.
accessibilitySupports: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
Evaluation and redesign may be written, storyboarded, dictated, or completed on a supplied criteria template.
trustedAdultNote: This course teaches health information and does not diagnose; direct urgent safety or health concerns to a trusted adult or qualified professional.

optionalReflection.prompt: Invite the learner to notice one safe, optional example of individual risk versus population-level risk in daily life. No purchase, account creation, photograph, recording, or private disclosure is required.

neverRequires: This task never requires body weight, height, BMI, or body-fat percentage.
This task never requires calorie counting or a diet or weight-loss goal.
This task never requires disclosing private medical history, a diagnosis, or sexual history.
This task never requires a photograph, video, or voice recording of the learner as proof.
This task never requires a public performance or an audience.

contentProvenance.objective: Explain individual risk versus population-level risk accurately using current, reliable health information rather than assumption or anecdote.
